tabs.title: Benefits and Problems
tabs.description: Evaluate what improved and what did not.

tabs.title: A Better Routine
tabs.description: Transfer the lessons to new situations.

questions.q: Why does the writer agree to the challenge so quickly?
choices: He has lost his mobile phone.
His class is going on a trip without internet.
He prefers sending long emails to friends.
He wants to demonstrate that living without messaging will be easy.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph identifies his wish to prove the task easy.

questions.q: What does repeatedly checking an inactive phone suggest?
choices: The phone is not working correctly.
The habit of checking is strong even without new messages.
The writer has forgotten how to make calls.
His teacher is sending him messages secretly.
questions.explanation: He checks dozens of times although there is no new message to find.

questions.q: Why is football training difficult to arrange during the experiment?
choices: The coach has cancelled the training.
He is not allowed to play sport after school.
The time is normally shared only in the team chat.
His parents have taken away his football shoes.
questions.explanation: The usual source of training information is unavailable.

questions.q: What surprised the writer about calling Karim?
choices: A short call solved the problem more quickly than a long chat.
Karim was unable to speak on the phone.
The coach had sent several emails instead.
They had to discuss the problem for hours.
questions.explanation: A two-minute call provides an answer without a long group conversation.

questions.q: What does the history-group episode show about a messaging-free week?
choices: The group no longer needs a history presentation.
The café is always quieter than the library.
Students never need to arrange meetings.
Important plans can change without reaching someone who is offline.
questions.explanation: The group changes the meeting place while the writer remains unaware.

questions.q: Why does the writer briefly feel like a tourist in his own class?
choices: He has recently moved from another country.
He misses shared news and jokes that his classmates know about.
He does not understand the history subject.
He cannot remember any of his friends' names.
questions.explanation: The funny video everyone discussed made him feel socially excluded.

questions.q: What does turning off notifications in some groups allow him to do?
choices: Choose which conversations need his immediate attention.
Avoid ever speaking to his classmates again.
Stop all messages from reaching his phone.
Replace every group chat with a phone call.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph shows him controlling when to respond.

questions.q: Why is calling his grandmother an example of changing his habits?
choices: She cannot receive any telephone calls.
She has joined his school media class.
He uses direct conversation where he once sent brief symbols.
He needs her to organise football practice.
questions.explanation: He replaces emoji messages with a call.

questions.q: A friend says the experiment proves messaging is harmful. What would the author reply?
choices: All chat groups should be closed permanently.
The main lesson is choosing when and how to communicate.
Voice notes are safer than phone calls.
The experiment showed there were no disadvantages.
questions.explanation: He explicitly rejects the claim that messaging itself is bad.

questions.q: When would a quick phone call be a sensible alternative to a long group chat?
choices: Whenever someone wants to share a long video.
Only when a friend has no phone.
When a message does not need an answer.
When a simple urgent question needs a clear answer.
questions.explanation: The quick call with Karim demonstrates efficiency for a specific question.
